#+TITLE: Panoptes Research: Optimizer Deep-Dive — Architecture + Algorithm Upgrades
#+DATE: 2026-08-12
#+RESEARCH_ANGLES: 6
#+STATUS: complete

* Executive Summary

The single highest-leverage finding of this run: **the current 0.9936 IoU baseline is measured against a deterministically-corrupted cost term.** Angle 02 verified at the dispatch's line numbers that the distance-map index formula (distance_map_metric.cu:27, `blockIdx.y + gridDim.x` instead of `blockIdx.y * gridDim.x`) mis-maps every block row, so the distance-map term of every DIRECT_DILATION oracle evaluation accumulates at the wrong pixels. That is the one live bug of the seven verified — the other six poison latent paths only. Fixing it and re-baselining (one single re-baseline after all behavior-neutral fixes land) is the prerequisite for every other decision in this run: variant switches, perf cuts, and gradient polish are all judged against a baseline that is not trustworthy until this lands. The gate (IoU ≥ 0.85) is far below the measured 0.9936, so the appearance arbiter stays, but measured IoU / per-px L1 / the 6.31 mm z gap are informational and expected to move.

The recommended course of action, in dependency order: (1) pin-first fixes per angle 02 (Tier-0 pins, then behavior-neutral fixes, then the distance-map index fix + one oracle re-baseline); (2) the measurement apparatus per angle 03 — the z-profile probe on the RunDirectStage injected-cost lambda (cheapest instrument that sees the z-weak axis) and the production-shaped multi-stage oracle through the plan-006 OptimizerRunDriver seam; (3) the ablation runner + ablation.json as the scoring surface; (4) the evidence-backed algorithm upgrade from angle 01 — **1-DTC-GL-gb** (GL two-step Pareto selection + globally-biased refinement control), scored by the harness before any production switch; (5) compute-perf cuts 0–4 per angle 05, gated on oracle green and bit-identical cost values; (6) the differentiable-polish stage per angle 06, GO-gated on the z-profile probe and an ablation arm. Architecture work (angle 04) is the enabler that flows through this path as additive cuts A–E rather than a separate project.

Two tensions the user should carry explicitly. First, **the variant switch cannot fix the z-axis**: angle 01's GL recommendation improves search efficiency in 6-D at n>4 budgets (≈60–72% fewer evaluations, high-evidence), but angle 06 shows the 6.31 mm z gap is a magnification observability limit in single-plane fluoro — no selection/partitioning scheme changes what is observable, and a depth channel does not fix it either; the real z remedies are biplane (already supported) or a known-geometry prior, and every z remedy is gated on angle 03's probe. Second, **perf cuts do not sacrifice determinism**: angle 05 verified every active cost-path reduction is an int atomicAdd (order-independent, value-deterministic), so async copies and iteration batching can preserve bit-identical results — the docs' "atomics aren't bit-reproducible" claim applies to the DRR float-atomic path, which is not in the DIRECT cost path; a pose→score diff harness makes the bit-identity claim checkable per cut.

The "12x fewer evals" polish thesis should be treated as a target to test, not a justification: angle 06's analysis puts the realistic win at ~1.5–3× in the leaf/refinement phase (trunk 20k dominates the budget), with the chamfer distance-map surrogate as the one smooth gradient signal that exists in the codebase. Everything else from the papers — DIRECT-GLh hidden constraints, 1-DTDV boundary sampling, analytic-AA occlusion gradients, DRR-photometric gradients, torch bridges — is conditional, deferred, or NO-GO per the evidence below, and each lands only through the harness.

* Key Findings

** Finding 1 — The baseline is contaminated by a live kernel bug; one re-baseline is the run's critical path
- Angle 02 verified all 7 cost-path bugs at the dispatch's line numbers. Only one is live in the oracle's cost (DIRECT_DILATION): the grid→pixel index formula at distance_map_metric.cu:27 uses `blockIdx.y + gridDim.x` where the correct formula is `blockIdx.y * gridDim.x`. For the 64×64 crop / 16×16-block case: crop rows 0–15 are never visited, rows 20–23 are visited twice; the metric is deterministic but wrong. The IoU 0.9936 / per-px L1 0.0207 / z gap 6.31 mm baseline therefore includes this corruption in every evaluation. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, Bug 5]
- The six other bugs are dead for the oracle: uninitialized min_dist (DD_NEW_POLE_CONSTRAINT.cpp:134, UB read — can be a signalling NaN), Y_dist ≡ X_dist no-op (117–120), sym_trap tibia x→z (sym_trap_function.cpp:106), always-Trunk stage guard (CostFunctionManager.cpp:46 — tautology, makes DIRECT_DILATION_T1's branch/leaf behavior unreachable), Mahfouz pointer-guard + int truncation (implant_mahfouz_metric.cu:324/446, :93/122), curvature stub returning 0 + per-stage allocation leak. A dead duplicate DistanceMapMetric call sits commented at DIRECT_DILATION.cpp:101–104. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, Bugs 1–4, 6–7]
- Pin-first recipes exist for every bug: Tier-0 pure-surface pins (extracted helpers, CPU references) where a pure surface exists, Tier-2 GPU-labeled pins where the pin must observe the cost itself. All pins are red or spec-documenting today — that is the R13 characterization pass, and it creates the pure surfaces the fixes plug into. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, "Fix order"]
- Execution consequence: fix all behavior-neutral bugs first (zero oracle impact), then the distance-map index fix, then a single oracle re-run and baseline.json re-baseline. Only one re-baseline happens. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, Phase 0–2]
- Cross-reference: angle 06 explicitly warns new polish kernels must NOT copy the buggy index formula; angle 03's Tier-0 metric references must encode the corrected formula as spec. All three angles converge on the same critical path. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "Feasibility verdicts"; angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, Tier-0 section]

** Finding 2 — Measurement-first is unanimous across all six angles: no algorithm delta before the apparatus
- The doctrine (plan 006: "no algorithm deltas before the measurement apparatus exists") is independently restated by every angle as its ordering rule: 01 "no variant touches production until the harness says so"; 03 is the apparatus spec itself; 04's cuts A–E are each pin-gated; 05 gates every perf cut on oracle green + bit-identity; 06 ships polish behind enable_polish_ and lands it only when the ablation arm wins at equal-or-lower cumulative budget. This is converged evidence, not a single source. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, 03-measurement-apparatus.org, 04-backend-architecture.org, 05-compute-perf.org, 06-differentiable-polish.org]
- The current oracle cannot see what needs measuring: 3 frames, trunk-only, flat budget 3000, backface OFF — NOT the production shape, leaf z-refinement never exercised by any test, and a SetCallOffset or dilation-scheduling regression passes today. The multi-stage oracle (20k→25k→30k→35k cumulative, per-stage dilation, tibia-after-femur, sym_trap) driven through the OptimizerRunDriver seam closes that gap, with a stage-bookkeeping gate (costCalls() must land on 20k/25k/30k/35k) that the flat oracle is blind to. [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "multi-stage oracle"]
- The driver seam is ready and green: OptimizerRunLaunch (by-value payload incl. 3 CostFunctionManagers), the OptimizerRunDriver interface, CreateOptimizerManagerRunDriver wrapping OptimizerManager untouched, and the controller's by-value relays (optimizedFrameRelayed) plus the oracle observation channel (costCalls/stageText/progress — "the oracle seam, M12"). One concrete seam gap was found: the typed Directive enum lacks SymTrap (needed for the tibia-ambiguity pass); a small seam addition is required. [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "multi-stage oracle"; local-recon.org]
- The ablation matrix must encode: 7 registered variants × budget shapes (production 20/25/30/35k, reduced CI shape, flat-3000 oracle shape) × dilation schedules (6/3/1 vs 6/4/1 — itself an ablation axis) × backface ON/OFF × frames {0,1,2}. Cost profile: flat-3000 is "a few minutes" → ~20–60 evals/s → full 35k production shape ~10–30 min/frame → full matrix is hours, hence manifest-driven subsets: reduced shape per-PR, full shape nightly. [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "ablation runner", "CI integration"]

** Finding 3 — The literature's highest-evidence algorithm upgrade is 1-DTC-GL-gb, and the current config is the literature's worst local-refinement regime
- Current repo config: original-DIRECT selection, ε=0, selecting ALL hull ties, 1-DTC-alike trisection on the largest denormalized side, L2 size measure. Jones & Martins 2021: ε=0 "spends so many evaluations refining local minima"; the empirical study: tie-all selection increases "global drag". The repo sits exactly in the worst regime the literature documents for a 20k–35k budget. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, Finding 1; https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07150; https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.14912]
- GL (two-step Pareto) selection beats IO/IA by ~60–72% on n>4 problems; budget crossover: IO wins ≤500 evals, N-DTC-IO best ~1000–4000, GL best ≥4000 — the 6-DOF search at 20k trunk lives far above the crossover. Partitioning: 1-DBDP best n>4 average but needs diagonal-bisection rework; 1-DTC best GKLS median and minimal code change; 1-DTDV catastrophic for interior optima (141,999 evals vs 919 on Levy10) — a trap unless the pose optimum is confirmed near the range boundary. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, Finding 2; https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.14912 §4.1–4.2, Table 3]
- Refinement control (Mathematics 2022, 10, 3760): every restriction except -gb hurts 1-DTC-GL on 287 DIRECTGOLib problems; -gb is the only one that never hurt and is best on expensive objectives (GPU silhouette with dilation 6/4/1 renders is expensive). Restrictions hurt worst when f* ≈ 0 — the silhouette-cost shape. ε-style restrictions are doubly contraindicated (the ε|f_min| window collapses as f_min→0). Landing variant: **1-DTC-GL-gb**, ε=0, L2 size kept, bit-identical defaults preserved behind an Options struct. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, Finding 4; https://epublications.vu.lt/object/elaba:143490244/143490244.pdf §3–§4]
- DIRECT-GLh (φ = f_min + d(x_min,x) surrogate for infeasible/NaN points) is near-zero cost — the distances are already computed by GL's two-step selection — and beats barrier/NAS methods 18/80 vs 29–53/80 failures on hidden-constraint problems. But the trigger is unverified: no finite-check exists anywhere in the C++ cost path, so whether the production GPU cost can emit NaN is unknown; angle 02's cost-path audit owns that check, and GLh is conditional on it. Today a NaN result poisons hull slope comparisons in ConvexHull (silent storage corruption). [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, Finding 3; https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.02205 §2.3, §4.2.1]

** Finding 4 — The z-weak axis is an observability limit, not an algorithm problem; the probe is the arbiter, and the real remedies are biplane or a known-geometry prior
- The 6.31 mm z gap (vs 0.16/0.08 in-plane) is the run's load-bearing research problem, converged from prior runs. The mechanism: a z shift is pure magnification — at ~1.1 m source distance a ±15 mm shift changes scale by <1%, inside the 6 px dilation tolerance; the dilated-overlap family is nearly flat in z. [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "z-profile probe"; local-recon.org]
- The z-profile probe reuses the RunDirectStage injected-cost lambda (optimizer_manager.cpp:1225+): sweep Δz ∈ {−15,…,+15} mm at fixed truth for the other 5 axes, 31 cost calls per (variant, dilation, frame) — a couple of minutes total on the RTX 3090 — and report valley_depth = (max−cost(0))/(max−min). A z-blind metric shows a flat or off-center curve. This is the cheapest instrument that sees the z-weak axis, and it gates every z remedy (SAME_Z weight calibration, chamfer reweighting, leaf refinement). [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "z-profile probe"]
- Angle 06's verdict on the depth channel: the machinery is ~80% present (DRR fill already interpolates perspective-correct z; dev_z_line_values_ buffer exists), but a front-surface z/w buffer does NOT make z observable in single-plane fluoro — there is no target depth to compare against, the gap is the magnification limit (no gradient changes what is observable), and NVDiffrast intentionally does not backprop through z/w (issue #70). The depth machinery is worth it only as: occlusion-aware visibility gradients, a synthetic-depth loss in the harness's self-supervised arm, or the z-line-integral in the ML/DRR pathway. The real z fixes are biplane (calibration_.convert_Pose_A_to_Pose_B + biplane branch already exist) and the known-geometry prior (implant constrained to a registered bone) — matching the prior-run ML angle's finding 8. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "depth channel"; https://github.com/NVlabs/nvdiffrast/issues/70]
- This is the dispatch-requested contradiction flag: angle 01's variant recommendations (1-DTC-GL-gb) optimize search efficiency but cannot move the z gap — the two are different kinds of improvement, and the probe is the instrument that separates them. A variant-switch win on the harness must not be mistaken for a z fix.

** Finding 5 — The cost path is sync-bound (structurally confirmed, magnitude unmeasured); 3 of 5 D2H syncs are trivially async-able, and int-atomics make bit-identical results achievable
- Per monoplane eval: ~15 kernel launches (8 render + 4 fast-implant-dilation + 3 distance-map) + 5 synchronous D2H cudaMemcpy, all on the default stream, zero streams/events anywhere in src/. The 5 syncs classify as: 2 structural mid-eval (bounding box at render_engine.cu:781–785; fragment_fill at :786–790 — removable only via kernel-level change) and 3 terminal (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289–290; distance_map_metric.cu:110–114, :115–119) — async-able now, all targets already page-locked. Cost nuance: the pairs share drains, so the real exposure is ~3 host-block windows per eval. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "Sync-point inventory"]
- The existing ms/call meter (optimizer_manager.cpp:1272–1278) uses clock() = process CPU time: it excludes GPU time AND sync-wait time, so it systematically under-reads a sync-bound pipeline and cannot arbitrate the item-8 claim. Fixing the meter (Cut 4) is required before any cut can be demonstrated to the user via the UI. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "The ms/call meter"]
- Determinism: every active cost-path reduction is an int atomicAdd/atomicSub on single counters — integer addition is order-independent, so identical launch configs + inputs ⇒ bit-identical scores. This resolves the docs' "atomics aren't bit-reproducible" claim: it applies to the DRR float-atomic path, which is NOT in the DIRECT cost path. Consequence: async terminal copies and iteration batching can be verified bit-identical by diffing a recorded pose→score sequence; Cut 3 (fragment-fill removal) must preserve per-thread work for threads < fragment_fill exactly. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "Determinism"]
- The DIRECT loop is sequential but each iteration's evals are pairwise independent (TrisectPotentiallyOptimal evaluates 2×N centers from a pre-loop snapshot) — batchable with replay-ordered bookkeeping, no GPU kernel rewrite. Constraint: FastImplantDilationMetric writes INTO the rendered buffer, so evals must be double-buffered (second render output + duplicate score buffers); biplane gets a free overlap (secondary camera buffers are separate). [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "The DIRECT loop is sequential", "In-place metric composition"]
- nvtx: declared in pixi.toml, zero instrumentation, and -DLIBNVTOOLSEXT is dead config; the nvtx3 header-only API compiles with no CMake/link change (toolkit include path already on jtml_compute). nsight-compute is in the lock; nsight-systems is not (needs pixi add). Per-eval timing data from Cut 0 replaces angle 03's derived 20–60 evals/s estimate. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "nvtx", "Measurement protocol"]

** Finding 6 — The polish stage is feasible only on a smooth surrogate; GO for chamfer-gradient polish, NO-GO for photometric/torch routes; the "12x" thesis is likely overstated
- The production DIRECT_DILATION cost is piecewise-constant in pose (binary silhouette + int reductions): finite differences on it give zero/garbage Jacobians; there is no gradient to polish through it. The surrogate already exists: DistanceMapMetric is a mean-chamfer loss with a Lipschitz image-space gradient ∇D, and its analytic gradient is the standard silhouette gradient dL/dθ = Σ ∇D(p)·(dp/dθ), needing only the per-pixel triangle-ID + barycentrics FillTriangleKernel already computes and discards (~10 lines + one float4 buffer to stage them). Published relatives: arXiv:1906.07870, arXiv:2501.14918. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "piecewise-constant", "smooth surrogate"]
- Feasibility verdicts: silhouette-gradient polish on the chamfer surrogate — GO (MVP = forward differences, 6 renders/step ~1 week; then analytic Jacobian + ∇D kernel, 1 render/step, +1 week; reuses Render(), uploaded distance maps, injected-cost lambda; float accumulation; match production backface=true and leaf dilation 1). NDC z/w depth buffer — feasible machinery but NOT a z fix; only as occlusion/ablation enabler. Analytic AA / occlusion-aware gradients — research increment after the MVP shows a win. Photometric DRR-intensity gradient — NO-GO for now (+3–6 weeks, low expected value). Finite-difference on the production cost — NO-GO. Torch bridge — NO-GO on design merit (autograd buys nothing for a 6-DoF static-STL scatter-add backward; and torch is already linked into jtml_compute — the ATen include in CostFunctionManager.h is a smell flagged to angle 04). [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "Feasibility verdicts"]
- Hybrid loop: trunk 20k → 2×branch 5k → leaf 5k → RunPolishStage(current_optimum) → optional DIRECT re-seed around the polished pose (Gablonsky locally-biased DIRECT / DIRECT+DF-local-search literature). Plug-in point mirrors RunDirectStage, no OptimizerRunLaunch signature change (reuses the leaf CostFunctionManager), budget-accounted (every surrogate + verification eval increments cost_function_calls_ so DIRECT-only vs DIRECT+polish is apples-to-apples at equal cumulative budget). Deliberately NOT routed through the Stage enum — the always-Trunk guard bug makes it unreliable. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "hybrid loop"]
- The "~12x fewer evals" thesis: unverified and structurally suspect — the budget is trunk-dominated (20k of 35k), so a 12x total claim requires shrinking the trunk (the ML-initializer pathway's job), while a gradient method plausibly converges the leaf refinement (~10^2 steps on a smooth surrogate) several-fold faster. Realistic expectation to measure: ~1.5–3× on the leaf phase + tighter final accuracy + lower frame-to-frame variance, at equal cumulative budget, reported data-profile style. GO condition for production: ablation arm shows ≥ the IoU gate at equal-or-lower cumulative budget with no per-axis regression; precondition: the z-profile probe shows the chamfer surrogate's valley is deeper than the dilated-overlap valley. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "12x thesis", "go/no-go"]

** Finding 7 — The backend seam evolution is additive-first and deliberately minimal: payload + StageScript + named derivations, no new layer
- The "backend" is already a stack of three seams (OptimizerRunDriver, Optimize()'s stage loop, DirectOptimizer's injected std::function). The target shape: OptimizerRunLaunch stays the single by-value payload, additively gaining the DIRECT Options struct; the stage sequence becomes a StageScript (vector of StageSpec: {kind, range, budget, repeat, cfm_index}) that the same Optimize() executor consumes; dilation/dark-silhouette derivation (DeriveStageCostParams) and the cost-adapter construction (BuildGpuCostAdapter) become named pure functions; DirectOptimizer's boundary stays std::function<double(const Point6D&)>. Explicitly NO RunBackend enum (the driver IS the run-level backend — the fake driver proves it), NO new CMake target, NO headless executor extraction until the multi-stage oracle demonstrates the driver seam insufficient, NO ML in the loop. [Source: angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "Target shape", "non-goals"]
- Dilation stays COST-owned: it is a derived property of the active CFM parameters (the "Dilation"/"dark_silhouette" name scan at optimizer_manager.cpp:237–345), not optimizer config — moving it would fork the single source of truth. The seam is the named pure function DeriveStageCostParams, called once in Initialize. This deliberately counters the dispatch's "dilation under optimizer configuration" framing. [Source: angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "Dilation stays COST-owned"]
- Payload evolution contract: additive fields are FREE (DirectOptimizer::Options defaulted = today's behavior; the fake-driver test records the whole launch by value and compiles unchanged); restructuring into nested sections is ONE gated signature-adaptation cut with the test updated in the same change; the driver interface, Initialize signature, by-value forwarding, the 8 binds, and the epoch/threadActive gate never change. Do NOT move the 3 CFMs to pointers (perf decision pending measurement; would change the fake-driver copy semantics). [Source: angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "Payload evolution contract"]
- The stage loop stays in Optimize() and becomes script-driven in place: the loop is the only algorithm policy among three interleaved work kinds (session/GPU state and signal emission stay in the manager). RunDirectStage stays the stage runner; its injected lambda becomes BuildGpuCostAdapter, with three consumers converging on it (production runner, z-profile probe, and oracle_test's hand-rolled twin at oracle_test.cpp:286–291). A future gradient-polish stage is one StageSpec + one new StageKind + its own runner branch — same seam, no StageRunner interface built today. R13 gap honestly recorded: Optimize()'s loop has no headless emission-order pin today (manager is GPU-bound); Cut B's evidence is parity + oracle green + jj diff relocation + the new pure-function pins. [Source: angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "script-driven loop", "R13 pin surface", "Migration sketch"]

* Contradictions and Open Questions

** Contradiction 1 — Dilation schedule: 6/3/1 (docs) vs 6/4/1 (code)
- Angle 02 resolved this with source evidence: the code implements 6/4/1 — settings_control.cpp:1201–1206 sets branch=4, leaf=1; settings_constants.h TRUNK_DILATION=6 / BRANCH_DILATION_DECREASE=2 / Z_SEARCH_DILATION=1 agree (consumed only by the experimental SettingsBridge); production OptimizerManager reads the per-manager "Dilation" runtime parameter. The 6/3/1 claim lives only in golden_oracle.org prose + baseline.json. Both agree on trunk 6 and leaf 1; the conflict is branch only (4 vs 3). Neither was ever runtime-captured (the flat-3000 oracle never exercises branch/leaf). Evidence favors 6/4/1 as implemented intent; docs are the stale artifact. Angle 03 treats the schedule as an ablation axis (data, not assumption); angle 04 requires DeriveStageCostParams to return exactly what the manager derives today. Resolution path: Tier-0 registry/constants pins → runtime probe → update golden_oracle.org + baseline.json to 6/4/1 or change settings_control.cpp:1204 to 3. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, "Dilation 6/4/1 vs 6/3/1"; angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "ablation runner"; angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "What Could Not Be Verified"]

** Contradiction 2 — Variant recommendations (angle 01) vs the z-axis (angles 03/06)
- Not a factual disagreement but a scoping tension the user must hold: angle 01's GL/1-DTC-GL-gb upgrade is about search efficiency at n>4, ≥4000-eval budgets — it changes which poses are tried, not what the cost can observe. The z gap is an observability limit (magnification, <1% scale change over ±15 mm at ~1.1 m). No selection/partitioning scheme, and no depth channel, changes that; the probe (angle 03) is the instrument that arbitrates, and the real z remedies are biplane/prior (angle 06). Do not read a harness win from the variant switch as evidence the z problem is addressed. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org; angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org; angles/06-differentiable-polish.org]

** Contradiction 3 — Perf cuts vs determinism: the docs' "atomics aren't bit-reproducible" claim vs the verified int-atomic cost path
- Angle 05 verified every active cost-path reduction is an int atomicAdd/atomicSub (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:145,147; distance_map_metric.cu:46–47; gpu_metrics.cu:129; iou.cu:66–72) — integer addition is order-independent, so results ARE bit-reproducible given identical launch configs and inputs. The order-nondeterministic float atomicAdd lives in the DRR fill (render_drr_engine.cu), which is NOT in the DIRECT cost path. Resolution: the docs' claim is stale; the determinism twin is a pose→score diff harness, and every perf cut (async copies, batching) is gated on the diff being empty. The one cut with a real determinism caveat is Cut 3 (fragment-fill kernel change), which must preserve per-thread work for threads < fragment_fill exactly. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "Determinism"; angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "ablation.json — determinism semantics"]

** Contradiction 4 — Backface culling: production ON vs oracle/label-generator OFF
- Production OptimizerManager constructs GPUModel with use_backface_culling=true; every oracle/parity path and the Study2Grid label generator use false (in-source comment: "BACKFACE CULLING APPEARS TO BE GIVING ERRORS"). The oracle must stay OFF: labels were generated OFF, and the frame↔label correspondence is pinned empirically by start-pose render IoU == 1.0 only under OFF; switching the oracle would break the gate against OFF-generated labels. The measured 0.9936 is an OFF-vs-OFF number and self-consistent. For production, ON is defensible for a closed opaque implant, but the two paths render different silhouette conventions where the STL is open/concave. Recommended evidence before touching production: (a) headless manifoldness check on KR_right_7_fem.stl (boundary edges == 0 ⇒ closed), (b) GPU-labeled ON-vs-OFF silhouette IoU at the golden pose (≈1.0 ⇒ immaterial; measurably <1 ⇒ deliberate reconciliation needed). Angle 06's polish must match the production backface config (true) for verification consistency — itself a tension with the oracle's OFF pin. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, "Backface divergence"; angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "Feasibility verdicts"]

** Contradiction 5 — Torch in the cost path: linked-but-banned
- torch is already linked into jtml_compute (machine_learning_tools.cpp is in the lib; CostFunctionManager.h includes <ATen/ops/div_native.h>) yet angle 06 says NO-GO on a torch bridge for polish (autograd buys nothing for the scatter-add backward; violates the "no torch in the cost path" design). The objection is design/convention, not dependency cost. The ATen include is a smell flagged to angle 04's architecture session. This is a latent inconsistency in the codebase, not a disagreement between angles. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "Feasibility verdicts"; angles/04-backend-architecture.org]

** Contradiction 6 — "12x fewer evals" (user's thesis) vs angle 06's ~1.5–3× leaf-phase estimate
- The thesis is unverified and structurally implausible as a total-budget claim: the trunk (20k of 35k cumulative) dominates, and polish cannot shrink the global phase. The honest target: evals-to-target-IoU at equal cumulative budget, data-profile style, with the win concentrated in leaf refinement. This is not a dispute about facts — it is the run's one explicitly low-confidence claim, to be arbitrated by the ablation arm. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "12x thesis"]

** Contradiction 7 — Split tie-break: repo (largest denormalized side) vs study (least-split-so-far)
- Angle 01: the repo's 1-DTC-alike rule ties break on the denormalized side length; the 2022 study's 1-DTC ties break least-split-so-far then lowest index. For anisotropic branch/leaf ranges (15,15,25,25,25,25; 3,3,15,3,3,3) the rules diverge; the effect on the 6-DOF search is unquantified. The battery should include an anisotropic-range probe using the actual trunk/branch/leaf ranges as box bounds. This is a mechanical-difference flag, not a correctness dispute — the repo's behavior is the pinned baseline either way. (truncated at 200 entries) ## README.md # DIRECTGOLib - DIRECT Global Optimization test problems Library ![languages](https://img.shields.io/badge/language-MATLAB,R-blue) ![release](https://img.shields.io/badge/release-v2.0-blue) ![OS](https://img.shields.io/badge/OS-windows,linux,macOS-blue) ![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue) ![contributions](https://img.shields.io/badge/contributions-welcome-greene) ## Table of Contents - [About](#about) - [Documentation](#documentation) - [Classification of Problems](#classification-of-problems) - [Composition of Library](#composition-of-library) - [Structure and Syntax](#structure-and-syntax) - [Example of the Initialization of Experimental Settings](#example-of-the-initialization-of-experimental-settings) - [Selection of Representative Instances](#selection-of-representative-instances) - [Cite Library](#cite-library) - [Feedback and Contributions](#feedback-and-contributions) - [Changelogs](#changelogs) - [v2.0 - (2024-09-01)](#v2.0-(2024-09-01)) - [v1.3 - (2023-06-15)](#v1.3-(2023-06-15)) - [v1.2 - (2022-06-06)](#v1.2-(2022-06-06)) - [v1.1 - (2022-04-26)](#v1.1-(2022-04-26)) - [References](#references) --- ## About An online collection called **DIRECTGOLib** stands as **DIRECT** **G**lobal **O**ptimization test problems **Lib**rary. The library presents a valuable collection of practical and test problems involving continuous variables. Initially the library created for benchmarking various DIRECT-type methods, but its current scope is suitable for any global optimization methods. Its main objective is to assist in creating and testing various numerical solvers for a wide range of global optimization problems. The **DIRECTGOLib** is an actively maintained open-source *GitHub* repository regularly updated with new problems from various optimization domains. All functions included have been thoroughly reviewed and corrected for errors such as specified wrong global minimum values or their locations, incorrect specifications of features and improper problem formulations. In addition, some measures have been taken into account to find exact duplicates or very similar functions. The library is entirely coded in the *MATLAB* programming language, ensuring accessibility and user-friendliness for the optimization community. The last version of **DIRECTGOLib v2.0**, is an updated version that builds upon the success of its predecessor, **DIRECTGOLib v1.3**. This latest iteration incorporates extensive expansion and restructuring efforts to ensure improved representation and better alignment with the current demands of testing global optimization algorithms. --- ## Documentation ### Classification of Problems Continuous global optimization problems from **DIRECTGOLib** are classified as follows: - [Box-constrained](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib/tree/main/Box) (324 problems in total) - [Linearly-constrained](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib/tree/main/Linear) (67 problems in total) - [Generally-constrained](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib/tree/main/General) (39 problems in total) - [Engineering problems](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib/tree/main/Engineering) (53 problems in total) We also separate problems coming from practical applications, which may involve various types of constraint functions. ### Composition of Library The problem library is a comprehensive collection of test problems gathered from various sources, ensuring a diverse range of scenarios and challenges. While there are numerous sources contributing to the library, there are a few that play a pivotal role in shaping its content. Users can refer to the respective problem's *MATLAB* file for any references not explicitly provided for further information and details. To provide an overview of the library's composition, the following table presents the number of essential parts that constitute its core: | \# | Identifier | References | Year | Problems | Problem Type | | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- | ---- | -------- | ------------------------------ | | 1 | Global Optimization Test Problems - Hedar list | Hedar[^1] | 2005 | 31 | Box-constrained | | 2 | Virtual Library of Simulation Experiments - Test Functions and Datasets | Surjanovic et al.,[^2] | 2013 | 50 | Box-constrained | | 3 | Hard benchmark functions for global optimization | Layeb,[^8] | 2022 | 18 | Box-constrained | | 4 | Global Optimization Benchmarks | Gavana,[^13] | 2013 | 193 | Box-constrained | | 5 | A literature survey of benchmark functions for global optimization problems | Jamil et al.,[^12] | 2013 | 167 | Box-constrained | | 6 | Real-parameter black-box optimization benchmarking 2009: Noiseless functions definitions - BBOB | Hansen et al.,[^5] | 2009 | 24 | Box-constrained | | 7 | Test functions for global optimization algorithms | Oldenhuis,[^14] | 2020 | 41 | Box-constrained | | 8 | Benchmark Functions for Single-Objective Optimization Based on a Zigzag Pattern - ABS | Kudela et al.,[^9] | 2022 | 8 | Box-constrained | | 9 | Special session and competition on single objective real-parameter numerical optimization - CEC 2014 | Liang et al.,[^10] | 2013 | 27 | Box-constrained | | 10 | Special session and competition on single objective real-parameter numerical optimization - CEC 2017 | Wu et al.,[^11] | 2017 | 20 | Box-constrained | | 11 | A Test-suite of Non-Convex Constrained Optimization Problems from the Real-World - CEC 2006 | Liang et al.,[^3] | 2006 | 13 | Generally/Linearly-constrained | | 12 | Introduction to global optimization | Floudas et al.,[^16] | 1999 | 20 | Generally/Linearly-constrained | | 13 | Derivative-Free Optimization and Applications Project | VAZ,[^4] | 2007 | 57 | Linearly-constrained | | 14 | Introduction to Global Optimization | Horst et al.,[^15] | 2000 | 7 | Linearly-constrained | | 15 | Parameter estimation in the general non-linear regression model | Gillard et al.,[^6] | 2017 | 6 | Engineering problems | | 16 | Engineering design examples | Ray et al.,[^7] | 2003 | 5 | Engineering problems | | 17 | CEC 2011 competition on real-world optimization problems | Das et al.,[^17] | 2010 | 19 | Engineering problems | | 18 | CEC 2020 competition on real-world optimization problems | Kumar et al.,[^18] | 2020 | 23 | Engineering problems | Please note that the table above is a summary and does not contain the complete list of all the references in the library. If you need more detailed information about a specific problem or its source, you can find detailed documentation and information directly in the corresponding *MATLAB* file. ### Structure and Syntax Understanding the syntax of coded problem m-files is provided with the following example of the `Tproblem.m`, for which the mathematical formulation is defined as follows: The global minimum is located at x = -1, f(x) = -n. (truncated at 200 entries) ## README.md # DIRECTGOLib - DIRECT Global Optimization test problems Library ![languages](https://img.shields.io/badge/language-MATLAB,R-blue) ![release](https://img.shields.io/badge/release-v2.0-blue) ![OS](https://img.shields.io/badge/OS-windows,linux,macOS-blue) ![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue) ![contributions](https://img.shields.io/badge/contributions-welcome-greene) ## Table of Contents - [About](#about) - [Documentation](#documentation) - [Classification of Problems](#classification-of-problems) - [Composition of Library](#composition-of-library) - [Structure and Syntax](#structure-and-syntax) - [Example of the Initialization of Experimental Settings](#example-of-the-initialization-of-experimental-settings) - [Selection of Representative Instances](#selection-of-representative-instances) - [Cite Library](#cite-library) - [Feedback and Contributions](#feedback-and-contributions) - [Changelogs](#changelogs) - [v2.0 - (2024-09-01)](#v2.0-(2024-09-01)) - [v1.3 - (2023-06-15)](#v1.3-(2023-06-15)) - [v1.2 - (2022-06-06)](#v1.2-(2022-06-06)) - [v1.1 - (2022-04-26)](#v1.1-(2022-04-26)) - [References](#references) --- ## About An online collection called **DIRECTGOLib** stands as **DIRECT** **G**lobal **O**ptimization test problems **Lib**rary. The library presents a valuable collection of practical and test problems involving continuous variables. Initially the library created for benchmarking various DIRECT-type methods, but its current scope is suitable for any global optimization methods. Its main objective is to assist in creating and testing various numerical solvers for a wide range of global optimization problems. The **DIRECTGOLib** is an actively maintained open-source *GitHub* repository regularly updated with new problems from various optimization domains. All functions included have been thoroughly reviewed and corrected for errors such as specified wrong global minimum values or their locations, incorrect specifications of features and improper problem formulations. In addition, some measures have been taken into account to find exact duplicates or very similar functions. The library is entirely coded in the *MATLAB* programming language, ensuring accessibility and user-friendliness for the optimization community. The last version of **DIRECTGOLib v2.0**, is an updated version that builds upon the success of its predecessor, **DIRECTGOLib v1.3**. This latest iteration incorporates extensive expansion and restructuring efforts to ensure improved representation and better alignment with the current demands of testing global optimization algorithms. --- ## Documentation ### Classification of Problems Continuous global optimization problems from **DIRECTGOLib** are classified as follows: - [Box-constrained](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib/tree/main/Box) (324 problems in total) - [Linearly-constrained](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib/tree/main/Linear) (67 problems in total) - [Generally-constrained](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib/tree/main/General) (39 problems in total) - [Engineering problems](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib/tree/main/Engineering) (53 problems in total) We also separate problems coming from practical applications, which may involve various types of constraint functions. ### Composition of Library The problem library is a comprehensive collection of test problems gathered from various sources, ensuring a diverse range of scenarios and challenges. ## Quick Overview

**DIRECTGO**: A new **DIRECT**-type *MATLAB* toolbox for derivative-free **G**lobal **O**ptimization[^29]. This toolbox provides a comprehensive suite of deterministic, derivative-free optimization algorithms tailored for various single-objective optimization problem types, containing box, linear, nonlinear, or hidden constraints.

The majority of the algorithms in this toolbox are implemented sequentially, utilizing either static[^1] or dynamic[^26] data structures. Additionally, the repository includes parallel implementations[^27] for certain specific algorithms. The toolbox is organized into two main components:

- **DIRECTGO.mltbx** - *MATLAB* toolbox package containing implementations of DIRECT-type algorithms, including an extensive [DIRECTGOLib](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib)[^28] library (maintained separately) of the box, generally constrained, and practical engineering global optimization problems, often used for benchmarking DIRECT-type algorithms.
- **DIRECTGO.mlappinstall** - A single *MATLAB* app installer ﬁle containing everything necessary to install and run the **DIRECTGO** toolbox, including a graphical user interface (GUI).

Additionally, we provide source files of all implemented algorithms in the [Algorithms/](Algorithms/) folder.

## History of DIRECTGO Versions

- **DIRECTGO** *v2.0.0 (pre-release)* incorporates the **GENDIRECT**  a generalized framework[^33] that unifies most of the DIRECT-type algorithms for box-constrained global optimization under a single approach.
- **DIRECTGO** [v1.2.0](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGO/releases/tag/v1.2.0) incorporates thirteen new algorithms introduced in[^31] and[^32]. With these additions, the total number of algorithms in **DIRECTGO** reaches 61.
- **DIRECTGO** [v1.1.0](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGO/releases/tag/v1.1.0) now comprises twelve additional algorithms introduced in[^30]. With these new additions, the total number of algorithms in **DIRECTGO** amounts to 48.
- **DIRECTGO** [v1.0.0](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGO/releases/tag/v1.0.0) version, as described in[^29], includes the implementation of 36 distinct DIRECT-type algorithms.

### DIRECTGO Quick Start Guide

After installation of the *MATLAB* toolbox (using **DIRECTGO.mltbx**), all implemented DIRECT-type algorithms and test problems can be freely accessed in the command window of *MATLAB*. Unlike GUI, algorithms from the command line require more programming knowledge, and configurations must be done manually. All algorithms can be run using the same style and syntax:

```matlab
1. f_min = algorithm(P);
2. f_min = algorithm(P, OPTS);
3. f_min = algorithm(P, OPTS, D);
4. [f_min, x_min] = algorithm(P, OPTS, D);
5. [f_min, x_min, history] = algorithm(P, OPTS, D);
```

The left side of the equations specifies the output parameters. After the termination, the algorithm returns the best objective value `f_min`, solution point `x_min`, and the history of the algorithmic performance during all iterations `history`. The information presented here is the iteration number, the total number of objective function evaluations, the current minimum value, and the total execution time.

On the right side, the algorithm name `algorithm` and at least one input parameter are needed to specify. The first one is the problem structure `P` consisting of an objective function:

```matlab
>> P.f = 'objfun';
```

If the problem involves additional constraints, they also must be specified:

```matlab
>> P.constraint = 'confun';
```

## Quick Overview

**DIRECTGO**: A new **DIRECT**-type *MATLAB* toolbox for derivative-free **G**lobal **O**ptimization[^29]. This toolbox provides a comprehensive suite of deterministic, derivative-free optimization algorithms tailored for various single-objective optimization problem types, containing box, linear, nonlinear, or hidden constraints.

The majority of the algorithms in this toolbox are implemented sequentially, utilizing either static[^1] or dynamic[^26] data structures. Additionally, the repository includes parallel implementations[^27] for certain specific algorithms. The toolbox is organized into two main components:

- **DIRECTGO.mltbx** - *MATLAB* toolbox package containing implementations of DIRECT-type algorithms, including an extensive [DIRECTGOLib](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGOLib)[^28] library (maintained separately) of the box, generally constrained, and practical engineering global optimization problems, often used for benchmarking DIRECT-type algorithms.
- **DIRECTGO.mlappinstall** - A single *MATLAB* app installer ﬁle containing everything necessary to install and run the **DIRECTGO** toolbox, including a graphical user interface (GUI).

Additionally, we provide source files of all implemented algorithms in the [Algorithms/](Algorithms/) folder.

## History of DIRECTGO Versions

- **DIRECTGO** *v2.0.0 (pre-release)* incorporates the **GENDIRECT**  a generalized framework[^33] that unifies most of the DIRECT-type algorithms for box-constrained global optimization under a single approach.
- **DIRECTGO** [v1.2.0](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGO/releases/tag/v1.2.0) incorporates thirteen new algorithms introduced in[^31] and[^32]. With these additions, the total number of algorithms in **DIRECTGO** reaches 61.
- **DIRECTGO** [v1.1.0](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGO/releases/tag/v1.1.0) now comprises twelve additional algorithms introduced in[^30]. With these new additions, the total number of algorithms in **DIRECTGO** amounts to 48.
- **DIRECTGO** [v1.0.0](https://github.com/blockchain-group/DIRECTGO/releases/tag/v1.0.0) version, as described in[^29], includes the implementation of 36 distinct DIRECT-type algorithms.

### DIRECTGO Quick Start Guide

After installation of the *MATLAB* toolbox (using **DIRECTGO.mltbx**), all implemented DIRECT-type algorithms and test problems can be freely accessed in the command window of *MATLAB*. Unlike GUI, algorithms from the command line require more programming knowledge, and configurations must be done manually. All algorithms can be run using the same style and syntax:

```matlab
1. f_min = algorithm(P);
2. f_min = algorithm(P, OPTS);
3. f_min = algorithm(P, OPTS, D);
4. [f_min, x_min] = algorithm(P, OPTS, D);
5. [f_min, x_min, history] = algorithm(P, OPTS, D);
```

The left side of the equations specifies the output parameters. After the termination, the algorithm returns the best objective value `f_min`, solution point `x_min`, and the history of the algorithmic performance during all iterations `history`. The information presented here is the iteration number, the total number of objective function evaluations, the current minimum value, and the total execution time.

On the right side, the algorithm name `algorithm` and at least one input parameter are needed to specify. The first one is the problem structure `P` consisting of an objective function:

```matlab
>> P.f = 'objfun';
```

If the problem involves additional constraints, they also must be specified:

```matlab
>> P.constraint = 'confun';
```

The second parameter is an optional variable, `OPTS` to customize the default settings. The last parameter is the bound constraints for each dimension/variable:

```matlab
D (i,1) ≤ x_i ≤ D (i,2), i = 1...n;
```

BUT the tie-break: equal-longest = equal-LL → paper: least-split-so-far (same LL...) hmm — "the coordinate that has been split the least times during the entire search process SO FAR" — that's a GLOBAL counter (total splits of that dimension across all boxes), not the box's own LL! The paper's tie-break is a global per-dimension split counter. The code: among equal min-LL dims, min(VAL.minas) — minas is a global per-dimension selection counter. Hmm — these are both global counters but count different events (total splits of dim across all boxes vs total times dim chosen as trisection side). For the box's own LL tie (equal LL), the global counters distinguish. So code and paper agree structurally (global counter tie-break, then lowest index via min-return-first).

Hmm OK wait, I need to double check one more subtlety: in the paper, "the coordinate that has been split the least times during the entire search process so far" — in DIRECTGO, is there such a global split counter? MSS.LL is per-box. VAL.minas is global per-dim selection counter. Is minas == "total splits of that dimension across all boxes"? Each time dimension j is selected as trisection side for a POH, LL(j) of that POH box increments AND minas(j) increments. So minas(j) = total number of times dim j was the trisection side globally = total splits of dim j (since every split of dim j happens via selecting it as side). Actually yes — every trisection in dim j corresponds to one selection of dim j. So minas(j) IS the total global split count of dim j. So the code's rule: min-LL (longest side) → min-minas (least globally split) → lowest index. EXACTLY the paper's rule! Great — the DIRECTGO implementation matches the paper's 1-DTC description precisely (modulo the trivial longest-side/least-LL equivalence in the unit cube).

Interesting — BUT: DIRECTGOLib problems are NOT unit-cube! Bounds are like [−32, 32] etc. DIRECTGO maps bounds to the unit cube (CC ∈ [0,1]^n, physical = a + (b−a)·cc). So all problems are searched in the unit cube; side lengths in unit space are 3^{−LL_j} regardless of physical ranges (the physical anisotropy is in the mapping, not the search geometry). So 1-DTC's "longest side" in unit space = least-split. OK. The DIRECTGO implementation uses the least-split rule throughout, matching the paper.

NOW — the repo's rule: TrisectPotentiallyOptimal uses `DenormalizeRange(sides).GetLargestDirection()` — the largest DENORMALIZED side. In the repo, sides are stored in UNIT coordinates (HyperBox6D sides are unit — the box geometry is unit; DenormalizeRange multiplies by 2·range). So the repo breaks ties by the largest PHYSICAL (denormalized) side — i.e., the dimension with the largest range contributes. For the trunk (all ranges 35), denormalized sides are all equal multiples — rule coincides with least-split... wait no: denormalized side_j = 3^{−LL_j}·(2·range_j). With all ranges equal (trunk 35,35,35,35,35,35): largest denormalized = smallest LL = longest unit side — coincides with 1-DTC least-split. For branch (15,15,25,25,25,25): the range anisotropy means a dim with range 25 and LL 1 (side 25·(2/3)) could exceed a dim with range 15 and LL 0 (side 15·2=30)... let's compute: unit side after k splits = 3^{−k}; denormalized = 3^{−k}·(2·range). Dim A: range 15, k=0 → 30. Dim B: range 25, k=1 → 25·(2/3)=16.67. So largest denormalized = dim A (range 15, k=0) even though dim B (range 25) has a LONGER unit side... wait no: dim A k=0 means unit side 1 → denorm 30; dim B k=1 → unit 1/3 → denorm 16.67. Largest denormalized side = A. And the least-split rule: A (LL 0 < LL 1). Same answer here. When do they diverge? When a high-range dim has been split more... e.g., dim X range 15, LL 0 → 30; dim Z range 25, LL 0 → 50. Largest denormalized = Z; least-split: both 0 → tie-break by global counter. In the very first iteration (LL all 0), branch box: denormalized sides = (30,30,50,50,50,50) → largest = the four range-25 dims (z,xa,ya,za) → tie among them → GetLargestDirection returns lowest index among the max = Z_DIRECTION (z is index 3 → wait, order is x,y,z,xa,ya,za; max_element == x first...). DIVERGE! The repo trisects z first (because z has the biggest range in branch), the study's 1-DTC trisects x first (lowest index).

Is that meaningful? The denormalized rule biases refinement toward the large-range dimensions (z in branch = 25mm, z in leaf = 15mm). function [minima, xatmin, history] = sGb_BIRECT(Problem, opts, bounds)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function   : sGb_BIRECT
% Written by : Linas Stripinis          (linas.stripinis@mif.vu.lt)
% Written by : Remigijus Paualvicius    (remigijus.paulavicius@mif.vu.lt)
% Created on : 04/29/2020
% Purpose    : DIRECT optimization algorithm for box constraints.
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% [minima, xatmin, history] = sGb_BIRECT(Problem, opts, bounds)
%       s         - static memory management in data structure
%       BIRECT    - BIRECT(BIsecting RECTangles) algorithm
%       Gb        - globally-biased
%
% Input parameters:
%       Problem - Structure containing problem
%                 Problem.f       = Objective function handle
%
%       opts    - MATLAB structure which contains options.
%                 opts.maxevals  = max. number of function evals
%                 opts.maxits    = max. number of iterations
%                 opts.maxdeep   = max. number of rect. divisions
%                 opts.testflag  = 1 if globalmin known, 0 otherwise
%                 opts.globalmin = globalmin (if known)
%                 opts.globalxmin = globalxmin (if known)
%                 opts.dimension = problem dimension
%                 opts.showits   = 1 print iteration status
%                 opts.ep        = global/local weight parameter
%                 opts.tighterLB = Use more expensive tighter LB (true/false)
%                 opts.tol       = tolerance for termination if
%                                  testflag = 1
%                 opts.balancedSampling = Perform balanced sampling (true/false)
%
%       bounds  - (n x 2) matrix of bound constraints LB <= x <= UB
%                 The first column is the LB bounds and the second
%                 column contains the UB bounds
%
% Output parameters:
%       minima  -  best minimum value which was founded
%
%       xatmin  - coordinate of minimal value
%
%       history - (iterations x 4) matrix of iteration history
%                 First column coresponds iterations
%                 Second column coresponds number of objective function
%                 evaluations
%                 Third column coresponds minima value of objecgtive
%                 function which was founded at iterations
%                 Third column coresponds time cost of the algorithm
%
% Original DIRECT implementation taken from:
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% D.R. Jones, C.D. Perttunen, and B.E. Stuckman. "Lipschitzian
% Optimization Without the Lipschitz Constant". Journal of Optimization
% Theory and Application, 79(1):157-181, (1993). DOI 10.1007/BF00941892
%
% Paulavicius, R., Chiter, L., and Zilinskas, J. "Global optimization 
% based on bisection of rectangles, function values at diagonals, and a
% set of Lipschitz constants" Journal of Global Optimization. (2018). 
% DOI 10.1007/s10898-016-0485-6 
%
% Paulavicius, R., Sergeyev, Y. D., Kvasov, D. E., & Zilinskas, J. 
% "Globally-biased BIRECT algorithm with local accelerators for expensive 
% global optimization" Expert Systems with Applications. (2020).
% DOI 10.1016/j.eswa.2019.113052
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
if nargin == 2, bounds = []; end
if nargin == 1, bounds = []; opts = []; end

% Get options
[OPTI, VAL] = Options(opts, nargout, Problem, bounds);

% Alocate sets and create initial variables
[VAL, MSS, RECT] = Alocate(OPTI, VAL);

% Initialization step
[OPTI, VAL, Xmin, Fmin, MSS, RECT] = Initialization(VAL, OPTI,...
    Problem, MSS, RECT);

while VAL.perror > OPTI.TOL                                 % Main loop
    % Selection of potential optimal hyper-rectangles step
    POH = Find_po(MSS.FF(1:VAL.I), Fmin, OPTI.ep, MSS.DD(1:VAL.I), VAL);
    
    % Subdivide potential optimalhyper-rectangles
    [MSS, VAL, RECT] = Subdivision(VAL, Problem, MSS, POH, RECT, OPTI);
    
    % Update minima and check stopping conditions
    [VAL, Fmin, Xmin] = Arewedone(OPTI, VAL, MSS, RECT);
end                                                         % End of while

% Return value
minima      = Fmin;
if OPTI.G_nargout == 2
    xatmin    = (abs(VAL.b - VAL.a)).*Xmin(:, 1) + VAL.a;
elseif OPTI.G_nargout == 3
    xatmin    = (abs(VAL.b - VAL.a)).*Xmin(:, 1) + VAL.a;
    history   = VAL.history(1:VAL.itctr, 1:4);
end
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% AUXILIARY FUNCTION BLOCK
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : Options
% Purpose   : Get options from inputs
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
function [OPTI, VAL] = Options(opts, narg, Problem, bounds)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Determine option values
if nargin < 3 && isempty(opts)
    opts = [];
end
getopts(opts, 'maxits', 1000,'maxevals', 100000, 'maxdeep', 1000,...
    'testflag', 0, 'tol', 0.01, 'showits', 1, 'dimension', 1, 'ep', 1e-4,...
    'balancedSampling', false, 'tighterLB', false, 'globalmin', 0,...
    'globalxmin', 0);

if isempty(bounds)
% Return the problem information.
    getInfo = feval(Problem.f);
    
% dimension
    if getInfo.nx == 0
        VAL.n = dimension;
    else
        VAL.n = getInfo.nx;
    end
    
    VAL.a = arrayfun(@(i) getInfo.xl(i), 1:VAL.n)'; % left bound
    VAL.b = arrayfun(@(i) getInfo.xu(i), 1:VAL.n)'; % right bound
    
    if testflag == 1
% minimum value of function
        OPTI.globalMIN  = getInfo.fmin(VAL.n);
% minimum point of function
        OPTI.globalXMIN = getInfo.xmin(VAL.n);
    end
else
    VAL.a = bounds(:, 1);               % left bound
    VAL.b = bounds(:, 2);               % right bound
    VAL.n = size(bounds, 1);            % dimension
    if testflag == 1
        OPTI.globalMIN = globalmin;     % minimum value of function
        OPTI.globalXMIN = globalxmin;   % minimum point of function
    end
end

OPTI.G_nargout = narg;     % output arguments
OPTI.MAXits    = maxits;   % Fmax of iterations
OPTI.MAXevals  = maxevals; % Fmax # of function evaluations
OPTI.MAXdeep   = maxdeep;  % Fmax number of side divisions
OPTI.TESTflag  = testflag; % terminate if global minima is known
OPTI.showITS   = showits;  % print iteration stat
OPTI.TOL       = tol;      % allowable relative error if f_reach is set
OPTI.ep        = ep;       % global/local weight parameter
OPTI.balancedSampling = balancedSampling; % Perform balanced sampling
OPTI.tighterLB = tighterLB;% Use more expensive tighter LB
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : BEGIN
% Purpose   : Create necessary data accessible to all workers
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
function [VAL, MSS, RECT] = Alocate(OPTI, VAL)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
tic                                     % Mesure time
VAL.time    = 0;                        % initial time
VAL.itctr   = 1;                        % initial iteration
VAL.perror  = 10;                       % initial perror

% alociate MAIN sets
z   = round(OPTI.MAXevals);
MSS = struct('FF', zeros(1, (z/2)), 'DD', -ones(1, (z/2)), 'LL',...
    zeros(VAL.n, (z/2)));

RECT = struct('p1', zeros(VAL.n, 1), 'p2', zeros(VAL.n, 1),...
    'c', zeros(VAL.n, 1), 'f1', zeros(1, 1), 'f2',...
    zeros(1, 1), 'fmin', zeros(1, 1), 'pmin', zeros(VAL.n, 1));

if OPTI.G_nargout == 3
    VAL.history = zeros(OPTI.MAXits, 4); % allocating history
end
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : Initialization
% Purpose   : Initialization of the DIRECT
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
function [OPTI, VAL, Xmin, Fmin, MSS, RECT] = Initialization(VAL, OPTI,...
    Problem, MSS, RECT)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
VAL.I = 1;                                        % evaluation counter
RECT(1).p1 = ones(VAL.n, 1)./3;                   % initial point p1
RECT(1).p2 = ones(VAL.n, 1).*(2/3);               % initial point p2
RECT(1).c = (RECT(1).p1 + RECT(1).p2)/2;         
RECT(1).f1 = feval(Problem.f, abs(VAL.b - VAL.a).*RECT(1).p1 + VAL.a);
RECT(1).f2 = feval(Problem.f, abs(VAL.b - VAL.a).*RECT(1).p2 + VAL.a);

if RECT(1).f1 < RECT(1).f2
    RECT(1).fmin = RECT(1).f1;
    RECT(1).pmin = RECT(1).p1;
else
    RECT(1).fmin = RECT(1).f2;
    RECT(1).pmin = RECT(1).p2;
end
Xmin = RECT(1).pmin;

[MSS.FF(1), Fmin, VAL.fMinBeforeImpr] = deal(RECT(1).fmin);
MSS.LL(:, 1) = ones(VAL.n, 1);

VAL.fMinNotImpr = 0;

if OPTI.tighterLB == true 
    % Calculate more expensive but tighter diameter
    RECT(1).v = VertexGeneration(VAL.n); 
    MSS.DD(1) = Diameter(RECT(1).v, RECT(1).p1, RECT(1).p2);

function [minima, xatmin, history] = sDISIMPLvGlob(Problem, opts, bounds)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function   : sDISIMPLvGlob
% Author 1   : Linas Stripinis          (linas.stripinis@mif.vu.lt)
% Author 2   : Remigijus Paualvicius    (remigijus.paulavicius@mif.vu.lt)
% Created on : 03/17/2020
% Purpose    : DIRECT optimization algorithm for box constraints.
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% [minima, xatmin, history] = sDISIMPLvGlob(Problem, opts, bounds)
%       s         - static memory management in data structure
%       DISIMPL   - DISIMPL(dividig simplices) algorithm
%       v         - Eevaluations are performed on the vertices of the simplices
%       Glob      - globally-biased
%
% Input parameters:
%       Problem - Structure containing problem
%                 Problem.f       = Objective function handle
%
%       opts    - MATLAB structure which contains options.
%                 opts.maxevals  = max. number of function evals
%                 opts.maxits    = max. number of iterations
%                 opts.maxdeep   = max. number of rect. divisions
%                 opts.testflag  = 1 if globalmin known, 0 otherwise
%                 opts.globalmin = globalmin (if known)
%                 opts.globalxmin = globalxmin (if known)
%                 opts.dimension = problem dimension
%                 opts.showits   = 1 print iteration status
%                 opts.ep        = global/local weight parameter
%                 opts.tol       = tolerance for termination if
%                                  testflag = 1
%
%       bounds  - (n x 2) matrix of bound constraints LB <= x <= UB
%                 The first column is the LB bounds and the second
%                 column contains the UB bounds
%
% Output parameters:
%       minima  -  best minimum value which was founded
%
%       xatmin  - coordinate of minimal value
%
%       history - (iterations x 4) matrix of iteration history
%                 First column coresponds iterations
%                 Second column coresponds number of objective function
%                 evaluations
%                 Third column coresponds minima value of objecgtive
%                 function which was founded at iterations
%                 Third column coresponds time cost of the algorithm
%
% Original DIRECT implementation taken from:
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% D.R. Jones, C.D. Perttunen, and B.E. Stuckman. "Lipschitzian
% Optimization Without the Lipschitz Constant". Journal of Optimization
% Theory and Application, 79(1):157-181, (1993). DOI 10.1007/BF00941892
%
% Paulavicius, R., and Zilinskas, J. "Simplicial Lipschitz optimization 
% without the Lipschitz constant". 59, 23�40 (2014) Journal of Global 
% Optimization. (2014). DOI 10.1007/s10898-013-0089-3 
%
% Paulavicius, R., Sergeyev, Y.D., Kvasov, D.E. et al. "Globally-biased 
% DISIMPL algorithm for expensive global optimization". J Glob Optim 59, 
% 545�567 (2014). DOI 10.1007/s10898-014-0180-4
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
if nargin == 2, bounds = []; end
if nargin == 1, bounds = []; opts = []; end

% Get options
[OPTI, VAL] = Options(opts, nargout, Problem, bounds);

% Alocate sets and create initial variables
[VAL, MSS] = Alocate(OPTI, VAL);

% Initialization step
[OPTI, VAL, Xmin, Fmin, MSS, Simpl] = Initialization(VAL, OPTI, Problem, MSS);

while VAL.perror > OPTI.TOL                                 % Main loop
    % Selection of potential optimal hyper-rectangles step
    [POH, VAL] = Find_po(MSS.FF(1:VAL.m), Fmin, OPTI.ep,...
        MSS.DD(1:VAL.m), VAL);

    % Subdivide potential optimalhyper-rectangles
    [MSS, VAL, Simpl] = Subdivision(VAL, Problem, MSS, POH, Simpl);
    
    % Update minima and check stopping conditions
    [VAL, Fmin, Xmin] = Arewedone(OPTI, VAL, MSS, Simpl);
end                                                         % End of while

% Return value
minima      = Fmin;
if OPTI.G_nargout == 2
    xatmin    = (abs(VAL.b - VAL.a)).*Xmin(:, 1) + VAL.a;
elseif OPTI.G_nargout == 3
    xatmin    = (abs(VAL.b - VAL.a)).*Xmin(:, 1) + VAL.a;
    history   = VAL.history(1:VAL.itctr, 1:4);
end
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% AUXILIARY FUNCTION BLOCK
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : Options
% Purpose   : Get options from inputs
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
function [OPTI, VAL] = Options(opts, narg, Problem, bounds)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Determine option values
if nargin < 3 && isempty(opts)
    opts = [];
end
getopts(opts, 'maxits', 1000,'maxevals', 100000, 'maxdeep', 1000,...
    'testflag', 0, 'tol', 0.01, 'showits', 1, 'dimension', 1, 'ep',...
    1e-4, 'globalmin', 0, 'globalxmin', 0);

if isempty(bounds)
% Return the problem information.
    getInfo = feval(Problem.f);
    
% dimension
    if getInfo.nx == 0
        VAL.n = dimension;
    else
        VAL.n = getInfo.nx;
    end
    
    VAL.a = arrayfun(@(i) getInfo.xl(i), 1:VAL.n)'; % left bound
    VAL.b = arrayfun(@(i) getInfo.xu(i), 1:VAL.n)'; % right bound
    
    if testflag == 1
% minimum value of function
        OPTI.globalMIN  = getInfo.fmin(VAL.n);
% minimum point of function
        OPTI.globalXMIN = getInfo.xmin(VAL.n);
    end
else
    VAL.a = bounds(:, 1);               % left bound
    VAL.b = bounds(:, 2);               % right bound
    VAL.n = size(bounds, 1);            % dimension
    if testflag == 1
        OPTI.globalMIN = globalmin;     % minimum value of function
        OPTI.globalXMIN = globalxmin;   % minimum point of function
    end
end

OPTI.G_nargout = narg;     % output arguments
OPTI.MAXits    = maxits;   % Fmax of iterations
OPTI.MAXevals  = maxevals; % Fmax # of function evaluations
OPTI.MAXdeep   = maxdeep;  % Fmax number of side divisions
OPTI.TESTflag  = testflag; % terminate if global minima is known
OPTI.showITS   = showits;  % print iteration stat
OPTI.TOL       = tol;      % allowable relative error if f_reach is set
OPTI.ep        = ep;       % global/local weight parameter
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : BEGIN
% Purpose   : Create necessary data accessible to all workers
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
function [VAL, MSS] = Alocate(OPTI, VAL)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
tic                                     % Mesure time
VAL.nn      = VAL.n + 1;
VAL.time    = 0;                        % initial time
VAL.itctr   = 1;                        % initial iteration
VAL.perror  = 10;                       % initial perror
VAL.I = 0; 

% alociate MAIN sets
z   = round(OPTI.MAXevals);
MSS = struct('FF', zeros(1, z), 'DD', -ones(1, z), 'CC', zeros(VAL.nn, z));

if OPTI.G_nargout == 3
    VAL.history = zeros(OPTI.MAXits, 4); % allocating history
end
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : Initialization
% Purpose   : Initialization of the DIRECT
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
function [OPTI, VAL, Xmin, Fmin, MSS, Simpl] = Initialization(VAL, OPTI,...
    Problem, MSS)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
V = VertexGeneration(VAL.n);
Simpl = VertexTriangulation(VAL.n)';
VAL.m = factorial(VAL.n);

% Calculate function values on all vertices V
for i = 1:length(V)     
    V(VAL.nn, i) = feval(Problem.f, abs(VAL.b - VAL.a).*(V(1:VAL.n, i)) + VAL.a);
    VAL.I  = VAL.I + 1;
end

if VAL.m == 1 
    VAL.I = VAL.nn; 
end

% assign function values from the vertex set V
for j = 1:VAL.m 
    for k = 1:VAL.nn 
        for i = 1:length(V)
            if (norm(Simpl(j).V(1:VAL.n, k) - V(1:VAL.n, i),2) == 0)
                Simpl(j).V(VAL.nn, k) = V(VAL.nn, i);
                break;
            end
        end
    end
end
% Find vertex with minimal function value
for i = 1:VAL.m
    fmin = min(Simpl(i).V(VAL.nn, :));  
    MSS.DD(i) = sqrt(sum(ones(VAL.n, 1).^2)); 
    MSS.FF(i) = fmin;     
end
MSS.CC(:, 1:length(V)) = V;
[Fmin, fminindex] = min(MSS.CC(VAL.nn, 1:length(V)));   % initial minima
Xmin = MSS.CC(:, fminindex);                            % initial point  

VAL.fMinNotImpr    = 0;
VAL.fMinBeforeImpr = Fmin;
VAL.Yaro_epsilon   = 0.01;

% Check stop condition if global minima is known
if OPTI.TESTflag  == 1
    if OPTI.globalMIN ~= 0
        VAL.perror = 100*(Fmin - OPTI.globalMIN)/abs(OPTI.globalMIN);
    else
        VAL.perror = 100*Fmin;
    end
else
    VAL.perror   = 2;
end

if OPTI.G_nargout == 3              % Store History
    VAL.history(VAL.itctr, 1) = 0;
    VAL.history(VAL.itctr, 2) = VAL.I;
    VAL.history(VAL.itctr, 3) = Fmin;
    VAL.history(VAL.itctr, 4) = VAL.time;
end
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : Arewedone
% Purpose   : Update minima value and check stopoing conditions
function [VAL, Fmin, Xmin] = Arewedone(OPTI, VAL, MSS, Simpl)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Fmin, fminindex] =  min(MSS.FF(1:VAL.m));
Xmin = Simpl(fminindex).V(1:VAL.n, 1);

if (abs(Fmin - VAL.fMinBeforeImpr) > VAL.Yaro_epsilon*abs(Fmin))
    VAL.fMinNotImpr     = 0;
    VAL.fMinBeforeImpr  = Fmin;
end

VAL.time = toc;

% minimum value of function

% minimum point of function
        OPTI.globalXMIN = getInfo.xmin(VAL.n);
    end

    VAL.b = bounds(:, 2);               % right bound
    VAL.n = size(bounds, 1);            % dimension

OPTI.MAXdeep   = maxdeep;  % Fmax number of side divisions
OPTI.TESTflag  = testflag; % terminate if global minima is known

% Function  : BEGIN
% Purpose   : Create necessary data accessible to all workers
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
function [VAL, MSS] = Alocate(OPTI, VAL)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
tic                                     % Mesure time
VAL.nn      = VAL.n + 1;
VAL.time    = 0;                        % initial time
VAL.itctr   = 1;                        % initial iteration
VAL.perror  = 10;                       % initial perror
VAL.I = 0;

MSS = struct('FF', zeros(1, z), 'DD', -ones(1, z), 'CC', zeros(VAL.nn, z));

    VAL.history = zeros(OPTI.MAXits, 4); % allocating history
end
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : Initialization
% Purpose   : Initialization of the DIRECT
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
function [OPTI, VAL, Xmin, Fmin, MSS, Simpl] = Initialization(VAL, OPTI,...
    Problem, MSS)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
V = VertexGeneration(VAL.n);
Simpl = VertexTriangulation(VAL.n)';
VAL.m = factorial(VAL.n);

% Calculate function values on all vertices V
for i = 1:length(V)     
    V(VAL.nn, i) = feval(Problem.f, abs(VAL.b - VAL.a).*(V(1:VAL.n, i)) + VAL.a);
    VAL.I  = VAL.I + 1;
end

if VAL.m == 1 
    VAL.I = VAL.nn; 
end

% assign function values from the vertex set V
for j = 1:VAL.m 
    for k = 1:VAL.nn 
        for i = 1:length(V)
            if (norm(Simpl(j).V(1:VAL.n, k) - V(1:VAL.n, i),2) == 0)
                Simpl(j).V(VAL.nn, k) = V(VAL.nn, i);
                break;
            end
        end
    end
end
% Find vertex with minimal function value
for i = 1:VAL.m
    fmin = min(Simpl(i).V(VAL.nn, :));  
    MSS.DD(i) = sqrt(sum(ones(VAL.n, 1).^2)); 
    MSS.FF(i) = fmin;     
end
MSS.CC(:, 1:length(V)) = V;
[Fmin, fminindex] = min(MSS.CC(VAL.nn, 1:length(V)));   % initial minima
Xmin = MSS.CC(:, fminindex);                            % initial point  

VAL.fMinNotImpr    = 0;
VAL.fMinBeforeImpr = Fmin;
VAL.Yaro_epsilon   = 0.01;

% Check stop condition if global minima is known
if OPTI.TESTflag  == 1
    if OPTI.globalMIN ~= 0
        VAL.perror = 100*(Fmin - OPTI.globalMIN)/abs(OPTI.globalMIN);
    else
        VAL.perror = 100*Fmin;
    end
else
    VAL.perror   = 2;
end

if OPTI.G_nargout == 3              % Store History
    VAL.history(VAL.itctr, 1) = 0;
    VAL.history(VAL.itctr, 2) = VAL.I;
    VAL.history(VAL.itctr, 3) = Fmin;
    VAL.history(VAL.itctr, 4) = VAL.time;
end
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
return

%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Function  : Arewedone
% Purpose   : Update minima value and check stopoing conditions
function [VAL, Fmin, Xmin] = Arewedone(OPTI, VAL, MSS, Simpl)
%--------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Fmin, fminindex] =  min(MSS.FF(1:VAL.m));
Xmin = Simpl(fminindex).V(1:VAL.n, 1);

if (abs(Fmin - VAL.fMinBeforeImpr) > VAL.Yaro_epsilon*abs(Fmin))
    VAL.fMinNotImpr     = 0;
    VAL.fMinBeforeImpr  = Fmin;
end

VAL.time = toc;

(a) **Abstract:** "This article considers a box-constrained global optimization problem for Lipschitz continuous functions with an unknown Lipschitz constant. The well-known derivative-free global search algorithm DIRECT (DIvide RECTangle) is a promising approach for such problems. Several studies have shown that recent two-step (global and local) Pareto selection-based algorithms are very efficient among all DIRECT-type approaches. However, despite its encouraging performance, it was also observed that the candidate selection procedure has two possible shortcomings. First, there is no limit on how small the size of selected candidates can be. Secondly, a balancing strategy between global and local candidate selection is missing. Therefore, it may waste function evaluations by over-exploring the current local minimum and delaying finding the global one. This paper reviews and employs different strategies in a two-step Pareto selection framework (1-DTC-GL) to overcome these limitations. A detailed experimental study has revealed that existing strategies do not always improve and sometimes even worsen results. Since 1-DTC-GL is a DIRECT-type algorithm, the results of this paper provide general guidance for all DIRECT-type algorithms on how to deal with excessive local refinement more efficiently."
